summary: Montanus was a second-century figure in Phrygia (Asia Minor), active around 165-175 CE, who with the prophetesses Priscilla (Prisca) and Maximilla founded the ecstatic-prophetic renewal movement known to its followers as the New Prophecy and to its opponents, and later generations, as Montanism. On the account of hostile heresiological sources, on which the surviving picture rests almost entirely, he prophesied in ecstasy, spoke as or for the Paraclete (the promised Spirit), announced new revelation, and taught a rigorous discipline and an imminent end. Montanus left no writings of his own, and this entry presents his reported teaching as attributed to his opponents, not as neutral fact.
description:
Montanus was a second-century Christian from Phrygia in Asia Minor whose activity is conventionally placed around 165-175 CE (some sources place the movement's beginning somewhat earlier). Together with two women, Priscilla (also called Prisca) and Maximilla, he founded a prophetic renewal movement that its adherents called the New Prophecy (he kaine propheteia) and that its opponents and later tradition named after him, Montanism. The movement emphasized continuing prophecy through the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit promised in the Gospel of John, along with new revelation, a strict moral and ascetic discipline (rigorous fasting, restriction or prohibition of remarriage, a readiness for martyrdom), and an imminent eschatology; the sources report that its adherents named the Phrygian towns of Pepuza and Tymion as, or as the site of, the New Jerusalem.

The decisive difficulty in describing Montanus is that he left no surviving writings of his own, and the picture of his person and teaching rests almost entirely on HOSTILE heresiological sources, that is, on the reports of those who opposed and condemned the movement. The principal witness is Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History Book 5, chapters 16-18, who himself quotes earlier anti-Montanist writers: an anonymous author (the Anonymous) and Apollonius. According to the Anonymous, as quoted by Eusebius (EH 5.16), Montanus, in the region bordering Phrygia, 'became beside himself, and being suddenly in a sort of frenzy and ecstasy, he raved, and began to babble and utter strange things', and the two women likewise 'talked wildly and unreasonably and strangely'; the Anonymous presents this ecstatic mode of prophecy as spurious and the movement's followers as 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'. Apollonius, again as quoted by Eusebius (EH 5.18), reports that Montanus 'taught the dissolution of marriage' and 'made laws for fasting', and that he named the Phrygian towns of Pepuza and Tymion 'Jerusalem'. These reports are the hostile testimony of the movement's opponents and are recorded here as such, not as a settled account of what Montanus in fact taught. A further, more sympathetic witness is Tertullian of Carthage, who in his later career embraced the New Prophecy and wrote in its defence; he is a friendlier source for the movement, but he too is a secondhand witness for Montanus himself, writing decades later and in Latin North Africa rather than from within the original Phrygian circle. Epiphanius of Salamis, in the fourth-century Panarion, preserves further, likewise hostile, material and some sayings attributed to the prophets.

Because the whole surviving portrait of Montanus is mediated through his opponents, and because no text in his own voice survives, modern historians such as Christine Trevett and William Tabbernee reconstruct the New Prophecy cautiously, distinguishing the movement's own self-understanding as a work of the Spirit from the heresiographers' framing of it as false prophecy and disorder. This entry follows that caution: Montanus's teaching, his ecstatic prophecy, his claim regarding the Paraclete, his discipline and eschatology, is presented throughout as reported by hostile sources and attributed to them, and the question of whether the New Prophecy was a genuine or a false prophecy is not adjudicated.
editorial_notes:
The crux of this entry, and the reason for its editorial caution, is that Montanus left NO surviving writings of his own and is known almost entirely through HOSTILE heresiological sources. The picture rests on the reports of his opponents: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History Book 5.16-18, who quotes the earlier anti-Montanist writers known as the Anonymous and Apollonius, and Epiphanius, Panarion. Accordingly, following the same handling as the ebionites, marcion, and sadducees entries, Montanus's reported teaching (ecstatic prophecy, the claim that he was or spoke for the Paraclete, the rigorist discipline, the imminent eschatology, Pepuza and Tymion as the New Jerusalem) is presented throughout as ATTRIBUTED, that is, as reported by his opponents, and never stated as neutral fact (neutrality #1, #2). Whether the New Prophecy was genuine or false prophecy is NOT adjudicated. Tertullian, who later joined the movement, is noted as a more sympathetic witness, but he too is secondhand for Montanus himself (later, in Latin North Africa, not from within the original Phrygian circle), so he does not give access to Montanus's own voice either.

Dates (fl. c. 165-175 CE) are approximate and disputed in the scholarship; the note records the uncertainty. Sourcing follows the three-lens model per neutrality #8, adapted to a figure known only through his opponents: (a) academic historians of early Christianity (Christine Trevett, Montanism: Gender, Authority and the New Prophecy, Cambridge University Press, 1996; William Tabbernee's studies of Montanist inscriptions and prosopography), rated medium; (b) the primary corpus, present here as HOSTILE primary witness read verbatim on an open page, namely Eusebius, EH 5.16-18, quoting the Anonymous and Apollonius, cited as such; (c) contemporary reception is covered by the same academic scholarship, and Tertullian is noted as a sympathetic but secondhand ancient witness. No encyclopedias, no tertiary or popular sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: because the entire picture is hostile-attributed and no non-hostile primary text in Montanus's OWN voice is readable, this entry is honestly capped at 'draft' now and is reviewed-eligible at best, not verifiable to a primary in his own voice, and it says so here. The one source rated high is the OPEN primary read line by line: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History Book 5, chapters 16-18, read verbatim at newadvent.org, where the load-bearing passages were confirmed word for word: the Anonymous's report that Montanus 'became beside himself, and being suddenly in a sort of frenzy and ecstasy, he raved, and began to babble and utter strange things' and that Priscilla and Maximilla 'talked wildly and unreasonably and strangely' (EH 5.16); the followers 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'; the village setting in the part of Mysia bordering Phrygia; and Apollonius's report that Montanus 'taught the dissolution of marriage', 'made laws for fasting', and named Pepuza and Tymion 'Jerusalem' (EH 5.18). This high rating attaches to what the open page actually says (that these opponents so reported), NOT to the truth of the charges. Trevett and Tabbernee (proprietary) are rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic. The relation targets montanism and tertullian (status verified) exist in the dataset; priscilla-and-maximilla and paraclete are dangling forward references, not yet separate entries.

lifespan.note: Second century CE; conventionally active (fl.) around 165-175 CE in Phrygia, though the sources are inconsistent and some place the beginning of the New Prophecy somewhat earlier (c. 157/172 are among the dates transmitted). Birth and death years are unknown and no precise dates are asserted; the movement's own chronology survives only through its opponents.

relations.note: Montanus, with the prophetesses Priscilla (Prisca) and Maximilla, founded the movement its adherents called the New Prophecy and its opponents named Montanism after him. This entry supplies the founder referenced by montanism; his teaching is attributed throughout to the hostile sources that report it.

Priscilla (Prisca) and Maximilla were the two prophetesses who, with Montanus, led the New Prophecy; the Anonymous quoted by Eusebius (EH 5.16) reports all three prophesying in ecstasy. Attributed to the hostile source. Dangling forward reference; not yet a separate entry.

Tertullian of Carthage embraced the New Prophecy in his later career and defended it, and is a more sympathetic witness to the movement than the heresiographers; but he wrote decades later in Latin North Africa and is a secondhand witness for Montanus himself. Attributed. The tertullian entry exists in the dataset (data/figures/christianity/tertullian.json, status verified).

On the report of the Anonymous quoted by Eusebius (EH 5.16), the followers of Montanus were 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete', the Spirit promised in the Gospel of John; the New Prophecy's emphasis on continuing revelation through the Paraclete is central to the movement as its opponents describe it. Attributed to the hostile source, not stated as fact. Dangling forward reference; not yet a separate entry.

sources.citation: Eusebius of Caesarea. Ecclesiastical History (Church History), Book 5, chapters 16-18. Translated by Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, Vol. 1. HOSTILE PRIMARY WITNESS, read verbatim on the open page: Eusebius quotes the anti-Montanist writers the Anonymous and Apollonius. Load-bearing passages confirmed word for word: Montanus 'became beside himself, and being suddenly in a sort of frenzy and ecstasy, he raved, and began to babble and utter strange things', with Priscilla and Maximilla who 'talked wildly and unreasonably and strangely' (5.16); the followers 'boasting that Montanus was the Paraclete'; the setting in the part of Mysia bordering Phrygia; and Apollonius's report that Montanus 'taught the dissolution of marriage', 'made laws for fasting', and named Pepuza and Tymion 'Jerusalem' (5.18). Cited as an attributed report by Montanus's opponents, not as neutral fact; rated high only for what the open page actually says (that these opponents so reported), not for the truth of the charges.

sources.citation: Trevett, Christine. Montanism: Gender, Authority and the New Prophecy. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996. The standard scholarly monograph on the New Prophecy, treating Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, the ecstatic prophecy, the discipline and eschatology of the movement, and the problem that the sources are overwhelmingly hostile. Academic history-of-early-Christianity lens.

sources.citation: Tabbernee, William. Prophets and Gravestones: An Imaginative History of Montanists and Other Early Christians (Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 2009); and Fake Prophecy and Polluted Sacraments: Ecclesiastical and Imperial Reactions to Montanism (Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 84; Leiden: Brill, 2007). Leading critical studies of Montanism drawing on the epigraphic evidence (Montanist inscriptions) alongside the literary sources, and on the ecclesiastical and imperial reaction to the movement. Academic lens; complements Trevett with the material-evidence angle.
